metadata.methods_description: Data were acquired using a 3 Tesla Philips Achieva dStream MRI scanner with 32-channel head coil. EEG was recorded at 5 kHz using 64-channel BrainAmp amplifiers (two 32-channel BrainAmp MRplus units) with hardware filtering (0.01-250 Hz). The 64-channel EEG comprised 63 head channels plus ECG. Additional physiological signals included 2 EOG, 4 EMG (Corrugator, Zygomaticus), and skin conductance channels. Auditory stimuli were presented via MR-compatible headphones. The category learning task comprised 180 trials with frequency-modulated sounds varying across five binary features (duration, frequency modulation direction, intensity, speed, frequency range). Participants indicated category membership via button press with trial-and-trial feedback. Resting-state fMRI was acquired for 10 minutes with eyes closed. Physiological signals (respiration, heart rate) were recorded at 100 Hz. EEG preprocessing included MR-artifact correction, bandpass filtering (0.3-125 Hz), and downsampling to 500 Hz. Raw data for optimized artifact correction are available upon request.

citation_details.title: FAIR m-BIDS: Advancing brain data utilization through multimodal and FAIR principles
citation_details.author: Seyed Mohammad Mirhosseini, Hoda Naseri, Bahaareh Siahlou, Mehran Panahi Arasi, Saeid Monazami Eslami, Ali Asghar Safaei
citation_details.abstract: In recent Datascience and AI studies, multimodality has become a key principle for achieving more accurate and dependable results. Managing multimodal data requires specialized platforms and structures to handle diverse data types from single subjects. The established BIDS (Brain Imaging Data Structure) standard faces limitations in supporting multimodal data, as each dataset is assigned to a single study with unique subject identities, preventing integration of multimodal data from the same individual across multiple studies. To address this limitation, this paper introduces FAIR m-BIDS (FAIR Multimodal Brain Imaging Data Structure), extending conventional BIDS by shifting granularity from dataset level to individual data entities. Each brain data file receives an independent GUId-Key (Global Unique Identifier Key), enabling researchers to select and integrate data items from different modalities and studies into customized multimodal datasets. The proposed structure enhances FAIR principles through improved findability, accessibility, interoperability, and reusability. Global identifiers enable tracking anonymized subject data across multiple datasets and modalities, while maintaining compatibility with conventional BIDS standards for advanced AI and neuroscience research applications.

citation_details.title: GFEX-EEG — Paper Analysis Code Bundle
citation_details.author: Michael McMahon, Michael Schukat, Enda Barrett
citation_details.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
citation_details.abstract: Analysis and figure-generation scripts reproducing the results, tables, and figures of the manuscript 'GFEX-EEG: Geodesic recovery of anatomical fiducials for MRI-free EEG source imaging' (McMahon, Schukat, Barrett). Includes per-cohort HTJ scoreboards, 3-point Procrustes and ICP baselines, ICP and PCAwarp A/B preprocessor evaluations, cohort-specific MLP training, the annotation-floor TOST equivalence analysis, the source-localization simulation, and figure scripts. Distinct from the GFEX-EEG toolbox (DOI 10.5281/zenodo.20580899). Reproduction requires the public cohorts (ds000221, ds000117/ds002718, ds004024, ds005795) and per-subject HTJ tags (available from the corresponding author on request).

citation_details.title: GFEX-EEG Validation Database: Brainstorm-tagged head models with manual helix-tragus-junction fiducials
citation_details.author: Michael McMahon, Michael Schukat, Enda Barrett
citation_details.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
citation_details.abstract: Processed Brainstorm head-model database used to validate the GFEX-EEG toolbox (Geodesic Fiducial Extrapolation for MRI-free EEG source imaging). For four per-subject EEG–MRI cohorts it provides the imported, defaced structural MRIs, the derived Brainstorm anatomical surfaces, and the manually-tagged helix-tragus-junction (HTJ) ground-truth fiducials (Brainstorm SCS fiducial structures, with SCS.LPA/RPA holding the left/right HTJ) that underlie every accuracy number reported in the GFEX-EEG manuscript. Each cohort is provided as a self-contained, Brainstorm-loadable ZIP archive (a complete Brainstorm protocol with anat/ and data/ folders): • LEMON — MPI-Leipzig Mind-Brain-Body (OpenNeuro ds000221 / NITRC Fcon_1000; Polhemus digitizer) • Wakeman-Henson — subject-correct "rescued" EEG–MRI pairing (OpenNeuro ds000117 + ds002718; Neuromag/Elekta) • Shirley Ryan AbilityLab — TMS-EEG-MRI-fMRI-DWI (OpenNeuro ds004024; BrainProducts CapTrak) • MULTI-CLARID — Leibniz Institute, Magdeburg (OpenNeuro ds005795) Ground-truth convention: the helix-tragus junction was tagged manually in Brainstorm's MRI viewer for every MRI-bearing subject; in each subject's anat/.../subjectimage_*.mat the fields SCS.LPA and SCS.RPA hold the left/right HTJ (not the conventional pre-auricular point), and SCS.NAS is the standard nasion. All reported GFEX-EEG errors are therefore true HTJ accuracy. Privacy: all structural MRIs are defaced. They are imported unmodified in facial content from source datasets that distribute them already defaced (LEMON; Wakeman-Henson; OpenNeuro-mandated defacing for ds004024; pydeface for ds005795), confirmed by source documentation and by direct visual inspection across all four cohorts. The brain is preserved; the identifiable facial surface is removed. Licensing: the GFEX-EEG curation layer in this record — the manual HTJ tagging, the Brainstorm head-model organization, and the selection/compilation — is released under CC BY 4.0. The underlying source neuroimaging data remain under their original public-domain dedications (LEMON: PDDL; Wakeman-Henson, Shirley Ryan, MULTI-CLARID: CC0) and are not relicensed. Please cite both this record and the original source datasets (see the included README.md). Related resources: GFEX-EEG toolbox (https://github.com/michaelmcmahon/GFEX-EEG; Zenodo concept DOI 10.5281/zenodo.20580898) and the GFEX-EEG paper-analysis bundle (https://github.com/michaelmcmahon/GFEX-EEG-paper-analysis; Zenodo concept DOI 10.5281/zenodo.20800437).

citation_details.title: Human alpha frequency and expression across the lifespan: a 2,172-participant electrophysiology-MRI atlas
citation_details.author: Sara Bonyadian, Arsalan Ghofrani, Mohammed Amin Miri, Russell Butler
citation_details.abstract: Hand-validated alpha measurements and T1-derived brain structure were brought together in more than 2,000 people from childhood to late adulthood. Alpha frequency and normalized alpha expression followed related, but not identical, courses through life. In the pooled lifespan model, cerebral white-matter volume most closely followed the rate of change of both alpha measures, but this ordering depended on the developmental observations supplied chiefly by HBN. Among adults, ordinary cortical anatomy accounted for little variation in IAF and only modest variation in normalized expression; the latter relation was largely one of cortical scale. These observations provide a guarded anatomical framework for studies of tract length, myelin-sensitive imaging, source localization, and longitudinal change.

citation_details.title: Geometric-Stochastic Multimodal Deep Learning for Predictive Modeling of SUDEP and Stroke Vulnerability
citation_details.author: Girish, Preksha, Mysore, Rachana, U, Mahanthesha, Kumar, Shrey, Annigeri, Misbah Fatimah, Jain, Tanish
citation_details.abstract: Sudden Unexpected Death in Epilepsy (SUDEP) and acute ischemic stroke are life-threatening conditions involving complex interactions across cortical, brainstem, and autonomic systems. We present a unified geometric-stochastic multimodal deep learning framework that integrates EEG, ECG, respiration, SpO2, EMG, and fMRI signals to model SUDEP and stroke vulnerability. The approach combines Riemannian manifold embeddings, Lie-group invariant feature representations, fractional stochastic dynamics, Hamiltonian energy-flow modeling, and cross-modal attention mechanisms. Stroke propagation is modeled using fractional epidemic diffusion over structural brain graphs. Experiments on the MULTI-CLARID dataset demonstrate improved predictive accuracy and interpretable biomarkers derived from manifold curvature, fractional memory indices, attention entropy, and diffusion centrality. The proposed framework provides a mathematically principled foundation for early detection, risk stratification, and interpretable multimodal modeling in neural-autonomic disorders.
